title: The Zen of Compensation
hook: The best pay system often does its work by becoming less distracting.
counterintuition: Intrinsic motivation is not an excuse to underpay people; unfair money keeps everyone staring at money.
tryThisNow: Look at one role and ask whether pay feels fair internally, fair externally, and simple enough to stop obsessing over.
keyTakeaway: Take money off the table by making pay fair, sufficient, and low-drama so autonomy, mastery, and purpose can breathe.

breakdown.fastRead: George Akerlof's gift-exchange idea points to a simple truth: pay carries social meaning. Red Gate Software and equity checks show why compensation has to feel fair before deeper motivation can take hold. Taking money off the table means reducing insecurity, resentment, and comparison, not pretending money is irrelevant. The rule is to pay enough, check internal and external fairness, and avoid incentive designs that turn complex work into bounty hunting.
breakdown.deepRead: The mechanism is attention: unfair pay colonizes the mind before autonomy or purpose can do much work. Once the baseline feels fair, work can be organized around autonomy, mastery, and purpose. Ignoring pay is naive, but overemphasizing contingent pay is corrosive. Good compensation design creates a stable floor for intrinsic motivation instead of competing with it. Compensation should be fair, sufficient, and hard to obsess over, because money becomes most useful when it stops dominating attention. Pay design should reduce resentment and avoid turning complex work into bounty hunting. Type I compensation pays enough and fairly enough to remove money as the central motivational issue.
breakdown.fullRead:
This principle runs opposite to a lazy reading of Type I motivation. The easy misread is that Type I workplaces should pay less because people are intrinsically motivated. The real principle runs the other way: unfair or inadequate pay poisons motivation, while healthy pay lets nonfinancial motives breathe.

George Akerlof's gift-exchange idea: Paying somewhat above market can function as a signal of trust and generosity. Workers may reciprocate with stronger effort, loyalty, and care.

Red Gate Software: The company moved away from traditional sales commissions toward healthy base pay. The change reduced pressure for narrow selling behavior and supported a broader customer-focused culture.

Internal and external equity checks: A pay system must feel fair compared with both coworkers and the outside market. Either kind of inequity pulls attention back to compensation and away from the work.

Fair baseline pay is a precondition for deeper motivation because perceived unfairness crowds out attention. Internal fairness compares pay among colleagues with similar responsibility and contribution. External fairness compares pay with similar roles in the broader labor market. Paying above average can reduce turnover, attract talent, and signal trust while avoiding constant incentive bargaining. Performance metrics should be broad, relevant, and hard to game. Modest variable rewards are safer than massive contingent prizes because they reduce narrowed focus and ethical pressure. Sales commissions can distort behavior when they turn customer relationships into short-term extraction.

Compensation occupies a special place because it can either stabilize motivation or consume it. The Type I approach begins by paying enough. If people feel underpaid, exploited, or insecure, appeals to purpose sound hollow and autonomy will not get much traction. Fairness has two dimensions. Internal fairness asks whether people are paid reasonably compared with colleagues who carry similar responsibility and contribution. External fairness asks whether pay matches the broader market. Paying above average can be a clean strategy because it attracts stronger people, reduces churn, and signals a relationship of trust. Akerlof's gift-exchange logic helps explain why generosity can be reciprocated rather than merely consumed. The approach also warns against oversized contingent rewards. Metrics should be wide, relevant, and difficult to manipulate, because narrow targets invite narrow behavior. Red Gate's move away from sales commissions illustrates the principle in a familiar setting: commission-heavy systems can motivate transactions while damaging trust, cooperation, and long-term customer value. The aim is neither ascetic nor lavish. It is to make money fair and quiet enough that people can focus on doing good work.
